stimulus.text: Jonathan Edwards read "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" in a flat voice, barely looking up from his notes, while the congregation came apart around him. George Whitefield, preaching the same message of human depravity and sudden conversion, performed with theatrical power — a loud, clear voice, sweeping gestures, and open-air crowds in the thousands.
stimulus.source_note: Background from the books: Edwards's flat delivery and Whitefield's theatrical preaching, as described in Barron's Chapter 4 and Princeton Review Chapter 6.

source: original; stimulus is a summary of the books' accounts
stem: What does the contrast between Edwards's and Whitefield's preaching best show about the Great Awakening?

options.text: That the revival's power lay in its message, which moved hearers whether read flat or performed.
That Whitefield's theatrical style was the only preaching method that ever worked in the colonies.
options.misconception: Edwards's flat reading moved his congregation to pieces; the theatrical style was not the only one that worked.

options.text: That Edwards's flat delivery proves his sermons were unpopular with colonial audiences at the time.
options.misconception: The passage says the congregation came apart around him; his sermons were famously powerful, not unpopular.

options.text: That the Awakening depended entirely on printed sermons rather than on any live preaching at all.
options.misconception: Both men preached live to crowds; print spread the message, but preaching carried the revival.

rationales.general:
1. Compare the two men. Edwards reads flat, eyes down; Whitefield performs, voice ringing across a field.
2. Compare the results. Both move their hearers to terror and tears.
3. Ask what the two methods share. The same message: helpless sinners, a sovereign God, conversion now.
4. Draw the conclusion. The power was in the message, not in one style of delivery.
Remember: flat reading and theatre both worked, because the revival ran on its doctrine — not on its staging.
rationales.A: Edwards and Whitefield could hardly have preached more differently — one flat and still, the other theatrical and loud — yet both moved hearers to terror and conversion. What they shared was the message: human helplessness, God's sovereignty, and the urgency of conversion. The contrast shows the revival's power lay in that doctrine, not in any single delivery style. Background: the Awakening spread through both settled pulpits and itinerant preaching, carried by the same theology.
rationales.B: Edwards's flat reading moved his congregation to pieces; the theatrical style was not the only one that worked.
rationales.C: The passage says the congregation came apart around him; his sermons were famously powerful, not unpopular.
rationales.D: Both men preached live to crowds; print spread the message, but preaching carried the revival.
